newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition calls election rerun a farce.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition calls election rerun a farce.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties, accusing the ruling Socialists of blatant election-rigging, launched fresh demonstrations against the restaging on Wednesday of local polls they say they have already won.
The opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition called for a boycott in Belgrade of the new round of voting, which it called a "farce" devised to seal results of poll fraud.
Wednesday's re-vote was organised after the Socialists led by President Slobodan Milosevic annulled opposition victories in Belgrade, Nis and other major towns in November 17 local polls.
The annulment of the Zajedno victories sparked outrage among opposition supporters and led to more than a week of peaceful protests that have drawn big crowds despite driving rain and sleet.
Several thousand university students, who have effectively shut down Belgrade faculties, marched through the city centre again on Wednesday in support of the opposition demands.
The students jeered at police with riot gear deployed along the route but no violence was reported.

Zoran Djindjic, an opposition leader, said the protests showed ordinary people were fed up with Milosevic's authoritarian rule and were eager for democratic reforms that have swept across the rest of Eastern Europe.
"We are melting the ice that has been forming over Serbia for 50 years. That is a long process," Djindjic told independent Belgrade radio B-92.
But it remained unclear if the Zajedno leaders could expand their protests and mobilise workers to strike.
The city electoral commission has warned the opposition to respect a law which bans campaigning for the last two days before voting.

The Zajedno coalition dismissed the warning and predicted a high turnout to protests in towns across the country as supporters realised Milosevic's Socialists would not concede defeat even at the municipal level.
The supreme court on Tuesday rejected a Zajedno appeal to cancel Wednesday's re-vote and uphold the results of second-round voting.
The state television station and the state-controlled newspaper Politika, Milosevic's main propaganda tools, reeked of eggs after demonstrators pelted the buildings for two days running.
In run-off polls on November 17, the opposition claimed victory in 15 of the country's 18 largest towns, including Belgrade.
But the electoral commissions -- all under the control of the Socialists -- then annulled almost all the wins, citing unspecified irregularities, and called another round of voting.

The United States has condemned the election annulments and senior envoy John Kornblum sent a letter of protest to Milosevic. The European Union postponed giving Yugoslavia preferential trade status granted to its neighbours.
Opposition organisers said the West had been slow to react as it views Milosevic as a guarantor of the peace agreement that ended fighting in Bosnia last year.
The scale of Zajedno's apparent win and subsequent public support appeared to have also surprised the leaders of the newly formed coalition.
"Yesterday we didn't know that there would be more than 100,000 people in the streets," opposition leader Zoran Djindjic told Reuters on Tuesday. "This is all new for us."
The opposition decided to contest the third round in three towns, Jagodina, Pirot and Uzice, where results had been annulled to a lesser extent, B-92 radio reported.
